name: Panpsychism
statement: Consciousness, in some basic form, may be a fundamental and pervasive feature of all matter.
statementAccent: a fundamental and pervasive feature of all matter
meaning: Panpsychism is the view that mind, mentality, or consciousness, in some form, is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of the natural world, so that all things, or at least all fundamental physical entities such as electrons and other elementary particles, possess some form of mental or experiential property. The name comes from the Greek pan, meaning all, and psyche, meaning soul or mind. Importantly, panpsychism does not usually claim that rocks or thermostats have rich, human-like thoughts; it attributes only some very basic form of experience to the fundamental constituents of matter, from which the richer consciousness of brains might be built. Panpsychism is offered as a solution to the hard problem of consciousness and the mind-body problem, a middle way between dualism and physicalism: if consciousness in some rudimentary form is a fundamental feature of matter, then one need not explain how consciousness emerges from wholly non-conscious ingredients, which some find unintelligible. The view has a long history, with precursors in Spinoza, Leibniz's monads, William James, and Alfred North Whitehead, and it is associated in contemporary philosophy with David Chalmers, Galen Strawson, and Philip Goff. Its central difficulty is the combination problem: how the tiny bits of experience in fundamental particles could combine to form the unified consciousness of a person. Panpsychism has seen a notable revival as a serious position in recent philosophy of mind.
mechanism: Panpsychism proposes that experience is not a late arrival that somehow emerges from non-experiential matter but is present, in a basic form, at the ground floor of reality. The motivating problem is the hard problem of consciousness: it seems deeply puzzling, some argue unintelligible, how full-blown subjective experience could arise from ingredients that have no experiential character at all, a worry Galen Strawson presses against radical emergence. Panpsychism dissolves this by holding that the fundamental physical entities already have some minimal experiential or proto-experiential property, so consciousness does not have to be conjured from nothing but is instead built up or combined from what is already there. A related and influential version is Russellian monism, which holds that physics describes only the structural and relational properties of matter, leaving its intrinsic nature unspecified, and proposes that this intrinsic nature is experiential, so that consciousness is the inner nature of the physical, compatible with the causal closure of physics. Constitutive panpsychism holds that the micro-experiences of fundamental entities constitute the macro-experience of a conscious being. The crucial challenge is explaining how many tiny subjects of experience could combine into the single unified subject that is a person, a difficulty William James raised early and that is now called the combination problem, and much recent work on panpsychism concerns whether and how it can be solved.

examples.text: Panpsychism holds that fundamental particles have some basic experiential property, so consciousness need not emerge from nothing.
One version holds that experience is the intrinsic nature of matter that physics, describing only structure, leaves unspecified.
The central difficulty is how the tiny experiences of particles could combine into the unified consciousness of a person.

variants.name: Constitutive panpsychism
variants.text: The view that micro-experiences of fundamental entities constitute the macro-consciousness of a conscious being.

variants.name: Russellian monism
variants.text: The related view that consciousness is the intrinsic nature of matter underlying physics' purely structural description.

whyItMatters: Panpsychism is important in contemporary philosophy of mind because it offers a bold and increasingly seriously considered response to the hard problem of consciousness, the puzzle of how subjective experience fits into the physical world. By proposing that consciousness in some basic form is a fundamental and pervasive feature of matter, panpsychism charts a middle course between dualism, which posits a separate immaterial mind and struggles with interaction, and standard physicalism, which struggles to explain how experience could arise from wholly non-experiential matter. If experience is already present at the fundamental level, then the emergence of consciousness need not be the seemingly unintelligible leap that motivates the hard problem. The view has deep historical roots and has undergone a notable revival, defended by prominent philosophers, precisely because the difficulties of the alternatives have made a fresh look at even a counterintuitive option worthwhile. Panpsychism also connects to foundational questions about the intrinsic nature of matter, which physics leaves open, and to debates about emergence and the structure of the physical world. Even for those who reject it, panpsychism sharpens the problem of consciousness and clarifies the options.

working.text: hold that fundamental physical entities already possess some minimal experiential property.
let the consciousness of complex systems be built from this basic experience rather than emerging from non-experiential matter.
explain how the tiny experiences of many particles could combine into the unified consciousness of a person.

limits: Panpsychism is a serious but far from settled position, and its central difficulty is severe. The combination problem asks how the many tiny subjects of experience attributed to fundamental particles could combine into the single, unified subject of experience that is a conscious person, and it is not clear that this can be made intelligible, a worry that traces back to William James and remains the main objection. Panpsychism is also strongly counterintuitive, since attributing any experience to electrons strikes many as implausible, though defenders stress that only a very basic form of experience is meant, not rich human-like thought, so the view should not be caricatured as claiming rocks have feelings. There are different versions, including constitutive panpsychism and Russellian monism, that face different problems, and the label panexperientialism is associated specifically with the Whiteheadian tradition.
misreadings: Panpsychism does not usually claim that rocks, thermostats, or particles have rich, human-like thoughts; it attributes only some very basic form of experience to fundamental entities. It is not a form of dualism positing a separate immaterial mind, but a view that experience is a fundamental feature of matter. And it is not free of difficulty, since the combination problem of how micro-experiences form a unified mind remains unsolved, so treating panpsychism as claiming rocks think, as substance dualism, or as an easy solution, misreads a counterintuitive but seriously considered view.
origin: The view that mind or consciousness is a fundamental and ubiquitous feature of nature, with roots in Spinoza, Leibniz, James, and Whitehead and a contemporary revival by Chalmers, Strawson, and Goff as a response to the hard problem.
